facts.claim: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep was discovered in 1953 by Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman.
facts.verification_notes: Aserinsky and Kleitman published the discovery of REM sleep in 1953 at the University of Chicago.

facts.claim: Sigmund Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams, proposing dreams as wish fulfillment, was published.
facts.verification_notes: Freud's 'The Interpretation of Dreams' was first published in November 1899 (dated 1900) and introduced wish fulfillment theory.

facts.claim: The activation-synthesis model, suggesting dreams arise from random brainstem signals, was proposed by Hobson and McCarley.
facts.verification_notes: Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley proposed the activation-synthesis model in 1977 at Harvard Medical School.

facts.claim: During a typical night, the brain cycles through REM sleep 4 to 5 times, each lasting longer.
facts.verification_notes: Healthy adults typically have 4-5 REM cycles per night, with later cycles progressively lengthening.

facts.claim: Approximately 95% of dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking.
facts.source: Hobson, J.A., Dreaming: A Very Short Introduction
facts.verification_notes: J. Allan Hobson's work frequently states that most dreams are forgotten soon after awakening, with the 95% figure often cited.

facts.claim: Dreams also occur during non-REM sleep, though they tend to be less vivid and story-like.
facts.source: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)
facts.verification_notes: NREM dreams do occur and are typically less elaborate and less vivid than REM dreams, as recognized by institutions like NINDS.

facts.claim: Sleeping after learning a task can double the likelihood of gaining insight into hidden rules.
facts.verification_notes: Wagner et al. (2004) in Nature demonstrated that sleep after training on a cognitive task doubles the probability of insight into hidden rules.

facts.claim: A 2008 study reported that about 12% of dreams are in black and white.
facts.verification_notes: The 2008 Murzyn study found that about 12% of dreams were black and white only in older adults who grew up with black-and-white TV; overall prevalence is much lower. The claim overgeneralizes the finding.

facts.claim: During REM sleep, brain glucose metabolism is comparable to that of wakefulness.
facts.verification_notes: Positron emission tomography studies (e.g., Maquet et al., Journal of Neuroscience, 1996) show REM sleep cerebral glucose metabolism similar to waking levels.

facts.claim: The final REM episode of the night can last up to 45 minutes, producing the longest dreams.
facts.verification_notes: Later REM periods in the sleep cycle can extend to 30-45 minutes or longer, consistent with sleep medicine guidelines.

facts.claim: Lucid dreaming, awareness of dreaming while dreaming, is experienced by about 55% of people at least once.
facts.source: Stumbrys et al., Consciousness and Cognition
facts.verification_notes: Stumbrys et al. (2012) meta-analysis in Consciousness and Cognition reported that approximately 55% of the population has experienced at least one lucid dream.

facts.claim: REM sleep plays a key role in processing emotional memories, reducing their intensity by the next day.
facts.verification_notes: Matthew Walker's research and his book 'Why We Sleep' (2017) describe REM sleep's role in overnight emotional memory processing and its calming effect.

hook_ideas: Every night, your brain produces a feature-length film—why?
We forget 95% of our dreams within minutes: what's the point of this nightly cinema?
Your brain is more active while dreaming than when you're awake—is it rehearsing for survival?
What if you could take control of your own dreams? The science of lucid dreaming.
misconceptions: Some people do not dream—actually, everyone dreams every night, even if they don't recall.
Dreams are meaningless random noise—many studies indicate roles in memory, emotion, and creativity.
Eating cheese causes nightmares—there is no solid scientific evidence for this folk belief.
Dreams only happen during REM sleep—non-REM dreams occur, but are less vivid.
All dreams are in color—about 12% of people's dreams are reported to be black and white.
key_sources: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)
Journal of Neuroscience, Nature, Consciousness and Cognition
